column4: People report that an enemy force has gathered against the believers; the report increases their faith, and they rely on God. This closely matches the section’s alarm of an approaching enemy and the response of taking precautions.
The believers return with favor and no harm touches them, completing the response to the warning in 3:173 and echoing the section’s protection from danger.
The command to take precautions and advance in groups gives another concrete military form of the source section’s warning about an enemy advance and the precautions that should follow.
The command to prepare strength against an enemy is a specific parallel to the section’s example of learning of an assault and making oneself ready.
The Prophet is told that the Quran warns its hearers and whoever it reaches; this specifies how the section’s alarm travels from one voice to its audience.
The Prophet is sent as a warner, and the verse names the companions of Hell; it joins the warning role to the fire outcome in the section.
The Book warns of severe punishment while giving good news to believers, joining the section’s alarm and its division between the fire-bound and the protected.
The believers’ abiding reward completes the good-news side introduced alongside warning in 18:2, complementing the section’s fire and shelter contrast.
Thamud’s denial is stated immediately before the rise of their most wretched person in 91:12, completing the section’s link between the ashqa and rejected warning.
The passage says people prefer the nearer life after describing the reminder-avoiding wretch; this makes explicit the preference behind the section’s turning away from warning and its fire.
The Hereafter is better and more lasting, completing 87:16’s contrast and clarifying why the section’s fire warning concerns a lasting end.
This verse says the disbelievers remain in the Fire without death or relief; the next verse recalls that a warner came, completing the section’s entry-and-warning sequence.
The servants of the Merciful spend neither extravagantly nor stingily; this sharpens the giver-versus-miser contrast that frames the section’s spared and fire-bound people.
The dwellers of the Garden are protected from the punishment of Hell; this is another direct use of the source-section root و ق ي for the pious kept away from fire.
The deniers are pushed toward Hell, a forceful entry scene for the fire that the section warns about.
They are told that this is the Fire they used to deny, matching the section’s sequence from warning to denial and punishment.
The inmates are asked whether the punishment is magic or whether they cannot see, continuing the exposure of the fire-deniers.
The command to burn in it uses the source-section root ص ل ي and directly describes enduring the flame.
The people of the left are given shade of black smoke; this apparent shelter is the opposite of the section’s protective shield, and the next verse states its failure.
That smoke-shade is neither cool nor beneficial, completing the failed-shelter image that reverses the section’s siper.
The passage identifies the condemned person as an astray denier, matching the section’s wretch who denied the warning before entering fire.
This denier’s reception is boiling water, the next stage of the punishment described before the burning in 56:94.
The verse names burning in Hell, using the source-section root ص ل ي and joining denial to fire.
Those who consume orphan wealth unjustly are said to eat fire and burn in the Blaze; this joins misuse of wealth to the source section’s wealth-hoarder and fire fate.
Disbelievers are burned in the Fire and their skins replaced so they continue tasting punishment, a direct instance of the source-section’s root ص ل ي and its enduring fire.
The verse contrasts the person cast into Fire with the one who comes safe on Judgment Day, closely matching the section’s wretch entering fire and the mindful person kept from it.

The disbelievers are brought to the Fire after enjoying worldly life and acting arrogantly; this makes a specific link between the section’s fire-bound person and the preference for nearer life described in 87:16.
Following God’s guidance means no going astray or being wretched; turning away leads into the hardship-and-fire sequence developed in 20:124–127 and the section’s ashqa contrast.
After God protects the givers from the Day’s evil in 76:11, this verse gives them gardens and silk, completing the protective reward linked to the section’s giver.
The human who is stingy when good reaches him sharpens the section’s contrast between the miser and the most mindful person spared from fire.
The righteous have a known share in their wealth, contrasting with the gatherer who hoards in 70:18 and the section’s fire-bound miser.
The wealth share is for the asker and deprived, specifying the giving that opposes the hoarding named just before the section’s fire scene.
The righteous affirm the Day of Judgment, the opposite of the section’s person who denies and turns away before the warning.
They fear their Lord’s punishment, giving the fear that motivates the section’s shield against the threatened fire.
The passage says no one is secure from the Lord’s punishment; this makes the section’s protective taqwa a needed response to the fire warning.
The people fail to urge feeding the poor, reversing the giving that marks the protected side of the section’s surah 92 contrast.
They consume inheritance greedily, extending the passage’s indictment of wealth-seeking before the Fire is brought near.
Their immense love of wealth specifies the worldly attachment behind the section’s gatherer who hoards before Leza calls.
Hell is brought near on that Day, completing the wealth indictment with the same approaching fire threatened in the section.
The person regrets not having sent deeds ahead for his life, sharpening the warning that worldly wealth cannot avail at the fall.
The condemned person is seized and bound, a concrete beginning to the punishment of the wretch who enters the section’s fire.
He is ordered into Hell, completing the seizure in 69:30 with the section’s central fire outcome.
The condemned did not believe in God, matching the section’s denied warning before the fire.
He did not urge feeding the poor, a specific reversal of the giving that marks the section’s protected side.
The sinner’s food in punishment is described as foul, continuing the fire-bound fate after the denial and withheld charity in 69:33–34.
Only sinners eat that punishment food, completing the section’s identification of the wretched person with the fire-bound end.
